steps.label: Conclusion (prediction = opinion)
steps.body: Widespread use of encryption software will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
steps.body: The most interesting, revealing source material for a biography will be unavailable to historians unless they have the necessary passwords.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Public figures' private correspondence and diaries are meant to be confidential when written, but they later become biographers' principal sources. In the future, most such documents are likely to be stored as encrypted text, which can be opened by password only.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion, read with one expectation in mind: the conclusion usually arrives before its support. Most of the time it is the first sentence or the sentence right after a pivot like "however."

So test the first sentence. It is a prediction: encryption "will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end." Nobody can observe the future, so a prediction is an opinion, and an opinion needs support. Ask: why should we believe that? The rest of the paragraph answers. Diaries and letters are the biographers' main sources. Those documents will likely be encrypted. So historians without passwords will lose the best material. Every later sentence is a reason for the first one.

Notice the chain has two levels. The "so" claim (historians will lose the revealing material) is itself a conclusion, supported by the encryption premise. But the argument does not stop there. Losing that material matters because it ends biographical writing. When one conclusion supports another, the one that supports nothing further is the main conclusion.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Find a meaning match for the first sentence: widespread encryption will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end. "Virtually to an end" means almost stopping, so a matching answer can say it will nearly stop, sharply decline, or cease.

Expect traps that restate the encryption premise or the "so" claim about historians losing access. Both sit on the path to the conclusion, but neither is where the argument ends up.

notes.body: This is the premise about storage: "most such documents are likely to be stored as encrypted text." Run the support test. Why does the author think biography will end? Partly because of this. A reason offered for the conclusion is evidence, not the conclusion. A also hardens "likely" into "will be."

This matches the first sentence piece by piece. "widespread use of encryption software" carries over unchanged. "will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end" becomes "will cause the writing of biographical history to decline significantly or cease." An almost-end is a significant decline, and an actual end is ceasing, so B covers the author's prediction without adding or dropping anything.

The move to repeat: once you have located the conclusion, put it in plainer words and look for the answer that says the same thing. On Main Conclusion, the correct answer is usually a paraphrase of one sentence, not a new idea.

This is close to the "so" claim: without passwords, historians lose the most revealing material. That claim is supported by the encryption premise, and it in turn supports the first sentence. Ask what it is for. Historians losing access is the reason biography will end. A claim that supports something else in the paragraph is not the main conclusion.

This is the last-claim trap. D restates the final sentence: the most interesting, revealing material "will be unavailable to historians unless they have the necessary passwords." It feels like the conclusion because it follows "so," and it is a conclusion, but only an intermediate one.

Run the support test in both directions. Why should we believe biography will end? Because historians will lose the best material without passwords. Why should we believe historians will lose it? Because the documents will be encrypted. The password claim sits in the middle of that chain. The first sentence is the only claim that is supported and supports nothing further, so it is the main conclusion.

The stimulus calls these documents biographers' "principal sources" and implies the most revealing material sits in them. E turns that into a ranking of all sources, which the author never states. Even as an implied idea, it would be background that explains why losing the documents matters. It supports the prediction; it is not the prediction.

old_steps.body: We just need a meaning-match for the first sentence.

old_notes.body: This answer restates a premise of the argument, not the main conclusion. The statement that most private correspondence and diaries will be stored as encrypted text is presented as a factual prediction about future technology adoption. It is one link in the causal chain that supports the main conclusion. The main conclusion is about the consequence of this encryption — the end of biographical history. This answer describes the cause (encrypted storage), not the effect (the end of biographical writing). In the argument's structure, this fact is offered as evidence for why biographical history will suffer, not as the main point the argument is trying to establish.

This answer accurately expresses the argument's main conclusion. The first sentence of the stimulus declares that the widespread use of encryption software will bring biographical history "virtually to an end." This is the broadest, most consequential claim in the argument — everything else supports it. The evidence about private documents being biographers' sources, the prediction about encrypted storage, and the intermediate conclusion about historians lacking passwords all feed into this overarching claim. This answer paraphrases the first sentence faithfully: encryption will cause biographical history to virtually cease. It captures the right claim at the right level of generality without overstating or understating the argument's position.

This answer says historians will probably not have access to much private correspondence and diaries of public figures in the future. While this is a reasonable inference from the argument, it functions as an intermediate conclusion or unstated implication — not the main conclusion. The argument's main conclusion is about the broader consequence of this inaccessibility: the end of biographical history. This answer describes a step in the causal chain (historians lose access) rather than the final result (biographical history ends). The main conclusion is the ultimate destination of the reasoning; this answer stops one step short.

This answer says biographers' access to interesting material will be determined by the availability of passwords. While this is implied by the argument, it is an intermediate conclusion, not the main conclusion. The argument uses this point — that password access will control information availability — to support its broader claim that biographical history will virtually end. This answer describes a mechanism or condition, not the ultimate consequence. Additionally, this is a classic "last-claim trap": test-takers sometimes select the last statement in an argument as the main conclusion simply because it appears at the end. But in this argument, the main conclusion appears in the first sentence, and the final sentence provides supporting detail.

This answer says public figures' private correspondence and diaries are the most interesting and revealing sources for biographical history. The argument does say that this material constitutes biographers' "principal sources" and refers to it as "the most interesting, revealing material." However, this is a background premise or assumption of the argument, not its main conclusion. The argument uses this claim to explain why the loss of access to encrypted documents would be devastating to biographical history. It is a building block, not the final structure. The main conclusion is about the consequence of losing access to these sources: the end of biographical history writing.

steps.label: Conclusion (clearly = opinion)
steps.body: Radioactive elements are still being created in the universe today (whether or not some of them were also created when the universe began).

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (So)
steps.body: If no new radioactive elements had been created after the universe began, almost no radioactive elements would be left in the universe today.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Radioactive elements are unstable, so most of them decay within at most a few million years into other, nonradioactive elements. Yet there is an abundance of radioactive elements in the universe today.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion before its support. It is usually the first sentence or the sentence after a pivot.

The first sentence hedges: radioactive elements "may have been created when the universe began." Here that "may" claim is a concession, not something the author sets out to prove. Then the pivot: "However, even if this occurred, these elements are clearly still being created in the universe today." "Clearly" marks the author's own view. Check it with the support test: why should we believe new radioactive elements are being created?

The rest of the paragraph answers that question. Most radioactive elements decay within a few million years. So if none had been made since the beginning, almost none would be left. But there are plenty left. Lined up:

No new elements created after the beginning → almost none left today
Not almost none left (there is an abundance)
So: new elements have been created

That is the contrapositive at work, and it lands exactly on the second sentence.

The final sentence starts with "So," which tempts us to call it the conclusion. It is a conclusion, but an intermediate one: it is drawn from the decay premise and then used to prove the second sentence. On Main Conclusion, the last sentence is rarely the answer, so check it before you trust it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for a meaning match for the second sentence: "these elements are clearly still being created in the universe today." Swap the pronoun for what it refers to: radioactive elements are still being created today. The answer does not need "clearly" or the "even if" clause.

Expect traps built from the "So" sentence, the decay premise, and the opening concession.

notes.body: The argument never states this. It is an inference you might draw from the decay premise, but a Main Conclusion answer has to restate the claim the author argues for. A is also about the wrong subject: the author's point is that new elements are being made today, not what became of the original ones.

This is the second sentence with the pronoun swapped out. "these elements" means radioactive elements, and "are clearly still being created in the universe today" becomes "are being created in the universe today." Dropping "clearly" and "still" does not change the claim.

Confirm with the support test. Everything else in the paragraph (the decay rate, the conditional, the abundance) answers one question: why believe new radioactive elements are being made? When a sentence after a pivot is backed by everything that follows, you have found the main conclusion.

This is the final sentence's conditional, and the "So" in front of it is the bait. It is a conclusion, drawn from the premise that most radioactive elements decay within a few million years. But the argument does not stop there. The author pairs it with the abundance of radioactive elements to prove something else: new ones must be forming. A claim that is supported and then used as support is an intermediate conclusion. When the last sentence opens with "so," ask whether it is used to prove anything further before you pick it.

This is the opening concession. "may have been created" is a possibility the author grants and then sets aside with "even if this occurred." Nothing in the paragraph argues for it. A claim the author concedes and moves past is background, not the conclusion.

This restates the third sentence: instability plus the decay timeline. It is the first link in the chain. Because the elements decay so fast, almost none would be left without new creation. The author offers it to prove something else, so it is support, not the point being supported.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (clearly = opinion)
old_steps.body: Radioactive elements are still being created in the universe today (whether or not some of them were also created when the universe began).

old_steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (So)
old_steps.body: If no new radioactive elements had been created after the universe began, almost no radioactive elements would be left in the universe today.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Radioactive elements decay within at most a few million years into other, nonradioactive elements. Yet there is still an abundance of radioactive elements today.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion and Role, we read the argument with a very unique reading protocol. After all, 90% of the time, on these two question types, the Main Conclusion comes earlier than the supporting ideas. Specifically, the conclusion will usually be
    - the very first sentence
    - some pivot/rebuttal idea
    This first sentence sounds tenuous, like maybe it could be an opinion we go on to support. But it also sounds factual and science-y, so the first sentence does not look too much like a conclusion. The second sentence gives us the telltale pivot we anticipate in Main Conclusion / Role: however. So we lean in ... aha! Is this pivot idea the conclusion? The Opinion Indicator "clearly" is our huge hint that yes, this is the conclusion. All we need now to confirm is to see that the paragraph is trying to convince us that radioactive elements are still being created today. And it does, via contrapositive logic. It says, "If no new radioactive were being created, there'd be almost no radioactive left in the universe. But there is an abundance of radioactive left in the universe." Thus, there are new radioactive being created. As always, on Main Conclusion, they are trying to trap students with Intermediate Conclusion, such as the "So" we see beginning the final sentence. And they try to get students to pick the last sentence as the conclusion, even though the last claim is only the conclusion on about 10% of Main Conclusion questions.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Let's look for the best meaning match we can find for the 2nd sentence: "Radioactive elements are still being created in the universe today".

old_notes.body: While this statement is probably true based on the argument's premises, it is never stated in the stimulus and is not the argument's main conclusion. The argument's conclusion is that radioactive elements are currently being created. The idea that any original radioactive elements have "probably decayed" is an inference one might draw from the premises, but the argument itself does not make this specific claim. The main conclusion is about ongoing creation, not about the fate of the original elements. Additionally, as an unstated inference rather than a direct claim in the argument, this cannot be the main conclusion by definition — the main conclusion must be something the argument actually asserts.

This is the argument's main conclusion, stated in the second sentence: "these elements are clearly still being created in the universe today." The word "clearly" signals the author's confident assertion — the claim the argument is designed to prove. Everything that follows serves this conclusion: radioactive elements are unstable (premise), they decay within millions of years (premise), if none were created after the beginning, almost none would remain (intermediate conclusion), but there is an abundance of them (factual observation). The instability, the decay timeline, the counterfactual scenario, and the abundance observation all converge as support for this single claim. This answer captures it accurately: radioactive elements are being created in the universe today.

This is an intermediate conclusion — a claim that supports the main conclusion while being supported by other premises. It appears near the end of the argument and functions as part of the logical chain: if no new radioactive elements were created, almost none would remain. But this conditional statement, combined with the observation that plenty exist, is the evidence that proves the main conclusion (that new elements are being created). It is also a common "last-claim trap" — appearing at the end of the stimulus, it can be mistaken for the main conclusion simply because of its position. But in this argument, the main conclusion appears earlier, and this statement serves it as a penultimate step in the reasoning chain. The test is always: does this claim support something else, or is it the final destination? This claim supports the "clearly still being created" conclusion.

The opening statement that radioactive elements "may have been created when the universe began" is background information — it introduces the topic and sets up the argument but is not the argument's conclusion. The word "may" indicates this is a concession or possibility being acknowledged, not an assertive claim. The argument immediately pivots with "however" and "even if this occurred" to state its main conclusion: these elements are clearly still being created today. The background concession establishes what is already known or plausible; the conclusion is the new claim the argument advances beyond that background. This statement is the starting point of the discussion, not its destination.

This is a factual premise that provides one piece of the evidentiary chain. The instability and decay rate of radioactive elements is presented as a scientific fact that supports the main conclusion. The argument's reasoning goes: elements decay quickly (this premise) -> if no new ones were made, none would remain (intermediate conclusion) -> but many exist (observation) -> therefore new ones are being created (main conclusion). A premise is a building block offered in support of a conclusion; it is not the conclusion itself. This statement is one of the foundation stones, not the structure built on top of them. The fact that it states an important scientific reality does not change its argumentative role as evidence rather than conclusion.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: It's a mistake to assume figuring out what caused the recession is essential to improving the economy.

steps.label: Evidence (after all)
steps.body: Corrective lenses were an effective treatment for myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion to come before at least some of its support. Most of the time it is the first sentence or a rebuttal after a pivot.

This one is the rebuttal. The first sentence is a fact: people are debating what caused the recession. Nothing supports it, and nothing needs to. Then the pivot: "It is a mistake, however, to assume..." That is the columnist taking a side.

To confirm, run the support test: why should we believe that answering the cause question is not essential? The next sentence opens with "after all," a support indicator, and gives a reason. Corrective lenses treated myopia well before anyone knew the cause was genetic. So a problem can be treated without knowing its cause.

The four support indicators to listen for are for, after all, because, and since (FABS). When one of them opens a sentence, the claim right before it is usually what it supports.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
When we have rebuttal-style conclusions, take an extra second to state the author's position in the words of the position being rebutted. For example, if we hear, "Some people think that ketchup is a vegetable. However, they're wrong," then the conclusion is "Ketchup is not a vegetable."

Here the opposing position is: "We need to figure out what caused the current recession in order to improve the economy. It's essential." The columnist says that is a mistake. It's not essential. You could improve the economy even if you never figured out what caused the recession.

Notice what kind of claim that is. "Essential" means required, so the columnist is saying knowing the cause is not necessary for improvement. Find the answer that says knowing the cause is not required, and nothing stronger.

notes.body: The columnist talks about one problem: the current recession. A turns that into a rule for every problem, and "never" makes it absolute. One myopia example can show that some fixes work without knowing the cause. It cannot show that no problem ever requires finding the cause.

B swaps necessary for sufficient. The columnist says knowing the cause is not essential: you can improve the economy without it. B says knowing the cause "would not necessarily enable people to find a solution": knowing it might not be enough. Those are different claims.

Test it. Imagine knowing the cause always led straight to a fix. B would be false, yet the columnist's point would survive, because the economy could still be improved without that knowledge. When a conclusion says something is not required, check that the answer is not really about whether it is enough.

This is the opening fact that sets up the debate. The columnist offers no reason to believe the question is hotly debated, and the rest of the paragraph does not try to prove it. A claim that nothing supports and that only introduces the topic is background, not the conclusion.

This is the second sentence translated. The columnist says it is "a mistake" to assume that answering the cause question "is essential to improving the economy." D says the same thing with "need not": you can improve the economy without ascertaining the cause of the recession.

The move to repeat: when the conclusion rejects someone else's view, restate it as the denial of that view (essential becomes not needed), then match. D also keeps the scope to the current recession, which is what keeps it from overreaching the way A does.

This is the evidence, introduced by "after all." The myopia example is the reason the columnist gives for the claim about the recession. Ask which claim it is offered to prove: that knowing a cause is not essential to a fix. Support for the conclusion cannot be the conclusion.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: It's a mistake to assume figuring out what caused the recession is essential to improving the economy.

old_steps.label: Evidence (after all)
old_steps.body: Corrective lenses were an effective treatment for myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion, we read the paragraph differently, because we know that instead of putting the conclusion at the end of the paragraph (the most common place), on Main Conclusion and Role we expect the conclusion to be earlier than (at least some of) the supporting ideas. Specifically, 90% of Main Conclusion questions have a conclusion that is
    - the First Sentence
    - a Rebuttal / Pivot idea
    This one did the second. The first sentence is just a fact. There's no support provided to defend the idea that people are hotly debating what caused the current recession. Then we see that magical however and think, "Is this the conclusion? Am I seeing the ol' Rebuttal / Pivot conclusion formula again?" To clinch our suspicion that this 2nd sentence is the Conclusion, we want to see that it's being Supported. The fact that the 3rd sentence begins with one of the four Support Indicators (FABS = for, after all, because, since) tells us that the 2nd sentence was definitely the conclusion.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: When we have Rebuttal style conclusions, we need to take an extra sec to state our author's position, using the wording of the position she's rebutting. For example, if we hear, "Some people think that ketchup is a vegetable. However, they're wrong", then we need to say that the Conclusion is "Ketchup is not a vegetable". So here the opposing position was that "We need to figure out what caused the current recession in order to improve the economy. It's essential." Our author is saying "No, it's not. That's a mistake. It's not essential. You could improve the economy, even if you didn't figure out what caused the current recession." Let's find the answer that best matches the meaning of the 2nd sentence.

old_notes.body: The columnist argues that knowing the cause of the recession is not essential to improving the economy — a narrow claim about one specific situation. This answer says "solving a problem never requires finding the root cause," which is a universal claim that goes far beyond what the columnist asserts. The word "never" transforms a specific observation into an absolute rule. The columnist does not say that finding root causes is never necessary for solving problems; the columnist says it is not essential in this particular case. The myopia analogy supports the possibility that solutions can precede causal understanding, but it does not prove that causal understanding is never needed anywhere. This answer overgeneralizes the conclusion to a degree the argument does not support.

This answer confuses "not essential" with "not helpful." The columnist says knowing the cause is not essential — meaning it is not a prerequisite for improving the economy. This answer says knowing the cause would not necessarily enable people to find a solution, which is a claim about whether causal knowledge is sufficient for a solution. These are different logical relationships. The columnist's point is about necessity: you do not need to know the cause to improve things. This answer is about sufficiency: knowing the cause might not be enough to improve things. The columnist is not arguing that knowing the cause would be useless or insufficient; the columnist is arguing that you can make progress without it. The conclusion is about what is not required, not about what might not work.

This answer restates a piece of background information from the stimulus, not the conclusion. The columnist opens by noting that the cause of the recession is "a hotly debated question" — this sets the stage for the argument but is not the argument's point. The conclusion is the columnist's own assertion that follows: it is a mistake to assume that answering this debated question is essential to improving the economy. Background facts describe the situation; the conclusion tells you what to do about or think about that situation. This answer identifies the scene-setting context rather than the argumentative claim built upon it.

This answer accurately captures the columnist's main conclusion. The argument's structure is: (1) background — the cause of the recession is debated; (2) conclusion — it is a mistake to assume that identifying the cause is essential to improving the economy; (3) evidence — corrective lenses treated myopia effectively before the genetic cause was known. The conclusion, paraphrased, is that one need not ascertain the cause of the recession to improve the economy. This answer matches that claim in scope and content. It does not overstate by claiming causal knowledge is never useful; it does not understate by merely restating the evidence or the background. It captures the core prescriptive insight: improvement can occur without prior identification of the underlying cause.

This answer restates the evidence, not the conclusion. The columnist uses the myopia example as an analogy to support the main point: just as myopia was treated before its cause was understood, the economy can be improved without knowing the recession's cause. The fact about corrective lenses is the supporting analogy — it serves the conclusion rather than being the conclusion itself. In argument structure, evidence supports the conclusion; the conclusion is what the evidence is offered to prove. The myopia example is marshaled to prove the columnist's broader point about the recession, making it evidence, not the main conclusion. Selecting this answer confuses the role of the illustration with the role of the claim it illustrates.

steps.label: Conclusion (this means that)
steps.body: We can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Railroads rely increasingly on automation. Since fewer railroad workers are needed, operating costs have been reduced. The chief competitor of railway shipping is shipping by truck, and no reduction in operating costs is predicted for the trucking industry.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion, expect the conclusion before at least some of the evidence. Usually it is the first sentence or a rebuttal after a pivot.

This one breaks the usual pattern. The first sentence is a plain fact about automation, and nothing argues for it. The second sentence is a claim about costs, supported by the worker reduction ("Since fewer railroad workers are needed"). The third sentence is the first one that sounds like the author looking ahead: "This means that we can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow." "We can expect" is a prediction, and "This means that" tells us it is drawn from what came before.

Run the support test. Why should we believe rail freight will grow? Because rail's costs went down. Then the last sentence adds a second reason after the conclusion: trucking, the main competitor, is not getting cheaper. So the conclusion sits in the middle, with support on both sides.

Phrases like "this means that," "this shows that," and "this suggests that" can mark a main conclusion just as well as "therefore." Don't assume the conclusion has to be the first or last sentence.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find the answer that matches the third sentence: rail freight volume is expected to grow. Watch for answers that restate the cost claim or the trucking premise. They are reasons for the prediction, not the prediction.

notes.body: This is the third sentence nearly word for word. "we can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow" becomes "can be expected to increase." Confirm with the support test. Lower rail costs and flat trucking costs are both reasons to expect more freight on rail, and the freight claim is not used to prove anything else. When a claim is supported from both sides and supports nothing further, it is the main conclusion, wherever it sits.

This links the first two sentences: automation means fewer workers. The stimulus treats that link as a starting point and uses the worker reduction to explain the lower operating costs. Ask what it is for: it feeds the cost claim, which feeds the freight prediction. A claim that only feeds the chain is not the conclusion.

This is the last sentence, and it is a premise. The author uses it to show that rail's cost advantage is real: trucks are not getting cheaper too. It gives a reason to expect rail freight to grow, so it supports the conclusion rather than being it. Don't pick the final claim just because it comes last.

This is the strongest decoy because it is supported. "Since fewer railroad workers are needed, operating costs have been reduced" gives a reason for the cost claim, so the cost claim is a conclusion of sorts. But the author does not stop there. "This means that" takes the lower costs and draws a further claim from them: freight volume will grow. The cost reduction is supported and then used as support, which makes it an intermediate conclusion. The main conclusion is the claim at the end of that chain.

This is background from the last sentence. It names the competitor so the cost comparison means something. Nothing in the paragraph argues that trucking is rail's chief competitor; the author states it and uses it. An unsupported fact that feeds the argument is a premise, not the conclusion.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (this means that)
old_steps.body: We can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: The chief competitor of railway shipping is shipping by truck. And while trucks don't have any predicted reduction in operating costs, operating costs for railroads have been reduced by automation.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
When we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we expect that about 90% of the time the conclusion will be in the First Sentence or be a Rebuttal. But in either case, we expect the conclusion to arrive earlier than the evidence. An "upside-down argument" in which you hear the conclusion and then hear support.
In this one the conclusion is actually in the middle, sandwiched between premises. It's shown to us via a less common Conclusion indicator phrase, "This means that".
In general, Main Conclusion and Role won't use easy/obvious indicator words like "Therefore, Thus, So" for the main conclusion. They'll use Opinion Indicators (like "probably / evidently / apparently" or just the future-tense, which indicates opinion). Or they might use stuff like "This reveals that, this shows that, this demonstrates that, this means that".

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: The hard part is done. We found the conclusion. Let's just find whatever answer matches the meaning of the 3rd sentence.

old_notes.body:
This is the main conclusion — the claim that every other statement in the argument is designed to support. The automation premise leads to fewer workers, which leads to lower costs, which — combined with trucking's inability to match those savings — supports this prediction about growing rail freight volume. This claim sits at the top of the reasoning chain: it receives support from everything else and provides support to nothing further.

You can confirm this by checking each other statement's role. "Railroads rely on automation" is a premise. "Fewer workers are needed" is supported by the automation premise and supports the cost claim — making it an intermediate conclusion. "Operating costs have been reduced" is another intermediate conclusion. "Trucking has no comparable cost reduction" is a premise. All of these funnel upward to support this single prediction. That is the hallmark of a main conclusion.

"Fewer railroad workers are needed" is an intermediate conclusion in the argument's chain. It is supported by the premise about automation (railroads relying on automated technology means fewer workers) and in turn supports the claim about reduced operating costs. Because it both receives and gives support, it cannot be the main conclusion. The main conclusion is the claim at the very top of the chain — the prediction about freight volume growth — which this statement helps prove but does not restate.

"No reduction in operating costs is predicted for trucking" is a premise — a factual claim offered to support the conclusion. It provides the competitive context: rail has lower costs, and trucking cannot match them. Combined with the cost reduction from automation, this premise supports the main conclusion that rail freight volume will grow. But a premise supports other claims; it is not the claim being supported by everything else. The main conclusion is the freight growth prediction, which this premise helps prove.

"Operating costs have been reduced as a result of automation" is an intermediate conclusion. It is supported by the chain of premises about automation and fewer workers, and it in turn supports the main conclusion about growing freight volume. Because it both receives support and provides support, it occupies a middle position in the argument — not the top. The main conclusion is the prediction about freight growth, which is what the cost reduction claim helps prove.

"The chief competitor of rail freight is shipping by truck" is a background premise. It identifies the competitive landscape so that the argument can make its point about rail's cost advantage. This factual claim supports the reasoning chain — it is not what the reasoning chain is designed to prove. The argument uses this fact about the competitive landscape to build toward its main conclusion about growing rail freight volume. A premise is the foundation, not the destination.

steps.label: Conclusion (not justified = opinion)
steps.body: The conclusion that ocean warming is a symptom of a more general, global warming caused by human-generated air pollution is far from justified.

steps.label: Evidence (it is known that)
steps.body: There are many natural cycles of ocean temperature changes that last 60 years or more.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we remind ourselves that 90% of the time, the conclusion will be the first sentence or it will be a rebuttal.
In this argument, the first sentence is clearly factual, not the author's opinion, so it's not a First Sentence Conclusion.
And when the second sentence begins with an attribution, "Some scientists claim", we would anticipate a Pivot into a Rebuttal.
Sure enough, we get "However, this conclusion is far from justified". The last sentence provides factual support. We can tell the last claim is factual because it is prefaced by "it is known that".

Confirm with the support test: why should we believe the scientists' conclusion is far from justified? Because natural cycles of ocean temperature can last 60 years or more, so a 15-year warming trend could be part of one. That is a reason to doubt the scientists' explanation, not proof that it is false. So the climatologist's conclusion is about the evidence: the human-pollution explanation has not been established.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Since our conclusion has a pronoun, "this conclusion is far from justified", we should take a sec and insert in the specific language the pronoun is referring to, as we did above when we wrote the Conclusion.
We should also limber up our synonym faculties by thinking, "What's another way to say this conclusion is far from justified?" Saying it's incorrect is too strong. It's more like "it's hasty to draw this conclusion / it's prematurely inferred / we don't have strong evidence for this".

notes.body: The climatologist states the 4-degree warming as a fact and does not argue for it. A also changes the claim: the stimulus never says some scientists found this evidence, and it never calls the warming "significant." The warming is the starting fact; the argument is about what explains it.

B is tempting because it points the same direction as the climatologist. But B says the warming is not a symptom of global warming. The climatologist only says that conclusion is "far from justified." Not proven is weaker than false. Natural cycles show the warming might be natural; they do not show it is.

Test it: could the climatologist accept that the warming really is caused by pollution, while still holding that the scientists have not yet justified saying so? Yes. So B overstates the conclusion. On Main Conclusion, match the author's strength, not just the author's side.

This is the rebuttal sentence with the pronoun filled in. "this conclusion" refers to the scientists' claim that the warming is a symptom of global warming caused by human-generated air pollution. C spells that out and keeps "is far from justified." Everything else in the paragraph serves that judgment: the warming is the scientists' starting fact, and the natural cycles are the climatologist's reason.

The move to repeat: when a conclusion contains "this" or "that," fill in what it points to, then look for the answer that keeps the author's exact strength. Here that strength is "not justified," not "false."

D says what the natural-cycle evidence suggests: the warming might be natural. The climatologist never says this outright, and even as an implied step it plays a supporting role. It is why the pollution explanation is far from justified. Support for the conclusion is not the conclusion.

This conditional never appears in the stimulus. It also adds a claim the climatologist does not need: that a natural cycle and human-caused global warming could not both be at work. The climatologist's point is about the evidence, that the pollution explanation is not justified, not a rule about which causes exclude each other.

old_notes.body:
The observation that waters have warmed by four degrees is a factual premise that the climatologist accepts and does not dispute. It is the starting point from which the climatologist builds an argument about what the warming means, not the destination of that argument. The climatologist's argument is not about whether warming occurred — that is taken as given by all parties.

Main conclusions are the claims arguments try to establish, not the facts they take for granted. Background facts serve as premises; the conclusion is the contested claim built on top of them. Here, the warming data is the foundation, and the "far from justified" judgment is the building erected upon it. The argument is about whether the warming justifies a particular interpretation (that it demonstrates global warming), not about whether warming occurred.

The climatologist does not flatly deny that the warming is a symptom of global warming. The climatologist's actual position is that the conclusion linking warming to global warming is "far from justified" — a claim about evidential sufficiency, not an outright denial. These are fundamentally different positions. "Far from justified" means the evidence is inadequate to support the global warming interpretation. It leaves open the possibility that global warming could be the cause; the argument merely contends that the evidence presented so far does not establish it. This mirrors the legal distinction between "not proven" and "proven false." The climatologist occupies the former position; this answer choice ascribes the latter. By upgrading cautious skepticism to categorical denial, this answer overstates the climatologist's claim.

The climatologist's argument contains several components: the acknowledged fact of ocean warming, the existence of natural temperature cycles, and the evaluative judgment that the global warming conclusion is "far from justified." The main conclusion is this last piece — the overarching claim that every other statement serves to establish. The argument's flow runs: natural ocean cycles could explain the warming (supporting premise), therefore the conclusion that warming is a symptom of global warming is far from justified (main conclusion). The warming data is a premise everyone accepts. The natural cycles point is the evidence. The "far from justified" judgment is the destination. To identify the main conclusion, ask: which claim is everything else aimed at establishing? Every element of the climatologist's argument funnels toward and supports this evaluative judgment about evidence quality.

The possibility that the observed warming is the result of a natural cycle is a supporting premise in the climatologist's argument. The argument's logical structure makes this clear: the natural cycle explanation is the reason the climatologist offers for the "far from justified" judgment. The reasoning runs: "Warming could be natural [premise], so the global warming conclusion is far from justified [conclusion]." To distinguish premises from conclusions, ask: "Is this statement being used to support something else, or is something else being used to support it?" The natural cycle point is deployed in support of the evaluative judgment.

Premises provide reasons; conclusions are what those reasons point toward. The natural cycle claim serves the conclusion — it is not the conclusion itself. It provides the evidential basis for the broader evaluative judgment that the global warming interpretation is "far from justified." The direction of support runs from this claim toward the main conclusion, not the other way around.

This conditional statement — if the warming is due to a natural cycle, then it is not a symptom of global warming — is a specific logical point within the argument, not the overarching claim that everything else supports. It functions as a narrower, more technical premise that feeds into the broader evaluative judgment. A conditional about the implications of natural versus anthropogenic causes is one building block in the argument's foundation.

The main conclusion should be the broadest, most encompassing claim that all other statements collectively support. The main conclusion is the "far from justified" judgment — the edifice constructed from those building blocks. When an argument contains both specific supporting claims and a broad evaluative conclusion, the broad evaluation is the main conclusion.

steps.label: Rossi's Argument
steps.body: Rossi states a general principle ("It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented") and applies it to children: since children's interests are sometimes different from their parents', children should have the right to vote.

steps.label: Smith's response (background)
steps.body: Smith concedes Rossi's point about different interests but raises a separate practical objection: children's conceptions and time horizons are too immature for voting responsibility.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The stem asks only about Rossi, so Smith's reply is background here. Read Rossi's two sentences as conclusion plus evidence.

Conclusion: children should have the right to vote.
Evidence: it is undemocratic for people to live under a government that does not represent their interests, and children's interests are sometimes different from their parents'.

Now characterize the evidence. The first sentence is not about children at all. It is a broad rule about all people: if your interests are not represented, your situation is undemocratic. The second sentence plugs children into that rule. Their interests can differ from their parents', so the parents' votes do not fully represent them, so by the rule children need a vote of their own.

That is one of the standard Method moves: state a general principle, then apply it to a specific case. Other common moves are analogy, counterexample, ruling out alternatives, and raising an overlooked consideration. None of those fits Rossi. There is no comparison case, no exception, and no rival explanation.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying Rossi relies on a general principle, or applies a broad rule to a specific group. Check every answer against Rossi's argument only. Smith's reasoning is the source of at least one trap.

notes.body:
Rossi's first sentence is a general rule: it is undemocratic for anyone to live under a government that doesn't represent their interests. Rossi then applies it to one group. Children's interests sometimes differ from their parents', so, by the rule, children need their own representation, which means the vote.

"Appeal to a general principle" is how the LSAT describes this move. When an argument opens with a broad "it is wrong / undemocratic / unfair to ..." claim and then applies it to a specific case, look for this answer.

Rossi speaks first, so there is no opponent yet, and Rossi never questions anyone's honesty or motives. Smith doesn't either: Smith grants Rossi's point about interests and disagrees on the merits. An answer about bad faith needs an accusation in the text, and there is none.

Rossi's argument is about what is democratic, not about what would happen if children voted. Rossi never predicts a single result. Smith's worry that children's conceptions are too simple comes closer to practical concerns, which is why C can feel familiar: it fits the other speaker better.

D can tempt because Rossi's argument is short and sounds like a pair of statements. But Rossi does give a rationale. The policy is "children should have the right to vote." The rationale is the principle (living with unrepresented interests is undemocratic) plus the fact (children's interests sometimes differ from their parents'). Test it: ask Rossi "why should children vote?" Rossi has an answer. An argument that substituted description for a rationale would only describe children or voting and never say why the policy follows.

This describes equivocation: one word used in two senses. The only term Rossi repeats is "interests," and it means the same thing both times: what is good for a person or group. With no shift in meaning, there is no equivocation.

old_steps.body: Rossi states a general principle ("It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented") and applies it to children: since children's interests are sometimes different from their parents', children should have the right to vote.

old_steps.body: Smith concedes Rossi's point about different interests but raises a separate practical objection: children's conceptions and time horizons are too immature for voting responsibility.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The question asks how Rossi's argument is structured. Rossi opens with a general principle (about democracy and representation) and then applies it to a specific case (children). That's an appeal to a general principle.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: Find the answer that describes Rossi as appealing to a general principle.

old_notes.body:
Rossi's first sentence is a general rule: it's undemocratic for *anyone* to live under a government that doesn't represent their interests. Then he applies it to one group. Children's interests sometimes differ from their parents', so, by the rule, children need their own representation, which means the vote.

"Appeal to a general principle" is how the LSAT describes this move. Whenever an argument opens with a broad "it is wrong / undemocratic / unfair to ..." and then applies it to a specific case, this answer is in play.
Rossi speaks first. He has no opponent yet, and he never questions anyone's honesty. (Smith doesn't do this either.)

Rossi's argument is about what's *democratic*, not what would happen if children voted. He never predicts any results. If anyone weighs practical consequences, it's Smith, who worries children's views are too simple for the responsibility. That's probably why this answer feels familiar: it describes the other speaker.

This is the most popular wrong answer, maybe because Rossi's argument is short and sounds like he's just stating things. But he does give a rationale. The policy is "children should vote." The rationale is the principle (unrepresented interests are undemocratic) plus the fact (children's interests sometimes differ). That's a reason, not a description.
This is the famous Equivocation flaw. The only term Rossi uses twice is "interests," and it means the same thing both times: what's good for a person. No shift in meaning.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: You can rely on Barr Motor Company to produce more winning automobiles than its competitors.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: (1) The pride at Austin Stables accounts for their success in producing more winning racehorses than any other stable. (2) For generations, Barr Motor Company has demonstrated similar pride. (3) That tradition of pride is not limited to horse racing.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The ad's structure is an analogy: pride causes Austin Stables to outperform competitors in horse racing; Barr has the same tradition of pride; therefore Barr should outperform its competitors in cars. The ad reaches its conclusion by drawing a parallel between two different industries based on a shared trait.

The sentence "Such a tradition of pride is not only found in the business of horse racing" is the bridge. It tells us the ad wants pride's payoff in one business to carry over to another. That is how an analogy works: what is true of one case is claimed for a similar case.

On Method, run the "argues X by Y" test on every answer: X has to match the conclusion and Y has to match the evidence. Here X is that Barr will beat its competitors, and Y is a comparison to a stable whose pride made it a winner. An answer that gets either half wrong is out.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Find an answer that describes the analogy-to-conclusion structure: an analogy is used to support a conclusion that Barr is superior to its competitors.

notes.body: The ad never mentions customers, repeat or otherwise. Its only evidence is pride and winning. A Method answer has to describe what the argument actually does, and nothing in the ad demonstrates anything about who comes back to buy.

Check both halves. Conclusion: "superior to its competitors" matches "produce more winning automobiles than our competitors." Evidence: "using an analogy" matches the Austin Stables comparison. Pride made Austin beat other stables; Barr has similar pride; so Barr will beat other car makers.

When an argument borrows a result from one situation and claims it for a similar one, expect the Method answer to say analogy.

C names something the ad does say: Barr has shown pride "For generations." But the ad only asserts it; nothing in the ad proves it. And it is a premise, not where the ad is going. The ad's point is that Barr will out-win its competitors. Asserting a premise and proving a claim are different moves, and a Method answer has to describe the argument's actual work.

The ad credits pride fully: pride "accounts for" Austin's success. It plays pride's role up, not down. Understating it would undercut the ad's own analogy, since Barr's case rests on pride being what makes the difference.

The ad never compares the ages of the two traditions. It says Barr has shown pride "For generations" and calls Austin's pride a tradition, but it never says which is older. The analogy needs the pride to be similar, not older.

old_steps.body: You can rely on Barr Motor Company to produce more winning automobiles than its competitors.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: (1) The pride at Austin Stables accounts for their success in producing more winning racehorses than any other stable. (2) For generations, Barr Motor Company has demonstrated similar pride. (3) That tradition of pride is not limited to horse racing.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The ad's structure is an analogy: pride causes Austin Stables to outperform competitors in horse racing; Barr has the same tradition of pride; therefore Barr should outperform its competitors in cars. The ad reaches its conclusion by drawing a parallel between two different industries based on a shared trait.

old_steps.body: Find an answer that describes the analogy-to-conclusion structure: an analogy is used to support a conclusion that Barr is superior to its competitors.

old_notes.body: Repeat customers are never mentioned. The ad talks only about pride and winning.
The analogy is Austin Stables: pride made it beat its competitors in horse racing. Barr claims the same pride, and concludes it will beat its competitors in cars.
This is the most popular wrong answer. The ad does mention Barr's long tradition of pride, but it only states it. Nothing proves it. "Asserting" and "proving" are different moves.
The ad leans hard on pride as the reason for Austin's success. Playing it down would undercut the ad's own analogy.
The ad never compares how old the two traditions are.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Pointing out that the correlation (people tend to gesture less when they talk about abstract rather than physical concepts) is far from universal is not enough reason to reject the researchers' claim.

steps.label: Evidence (because)
steps.body: Some people perceive words like "comprehension" as expressing a physical action, like grasping something, rather than a state of understanding, which is abstract.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with what the author is responding to. Researchers say people tend to gesture less when they talk about abstract concepts. A critic could point out exceptions: people who gesture while discussing something abstract. The author says exceptions like that are not enough to throw out the claim.

Why not? Because some of the exceptions may not be exceptions at all. Take someone who gestures while talking about comprehension. That looks like a strike against the researchers, since comprehension, as a state of understanding, is abstract. But if that person thinks of comprehension as grasping something, a physical action, then the person is talking about a physical concept, and gesturing is exactly what the researchers' claim predicts.

So the author keeps the generalization and explains away the counterevidence. The cases that seem to break the pattern are reclassified using a fact about how people perceive words. Notice that the author never says the correlation is universal and never brings in new support for it. The job is defensive: show that the apparent exceptions do not hurt the claim.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Use "argues X by Y" on every answer. X should match the conclusion: the researchers' claim survives the objection that the correlation is far from universal. Y should match the evidence: a fact about how some people perceive certain words.

In Method terms, the author answers a counterexample by giving it an alternate explanation that fits the rule. So look for something like: "uses a fact about how people perceive words to show that apparent exceptions are consistent with the generalization."

notes.body: A is tempting because the evidence really does turn on a word with two readings: comprehension as grasping or as understanding. But check the X half. The author does not try to show the correlation is universal. The argument never disputes that it is "far from universal" and claims only that this is "insufficient reason to reject the researchers’ claim." A tendency can hold without being universal. An answer that gets the goal of the argument wrong fails even when its method half sounds right.

The fact the author cites is about "some people," not everyone, so it is not a universal generalization. And it is not offered as fresh support for a claim about gestures. It is offered to explain why certain exceptions do not count against the researchers' claim.

Match it piece by piece. "citing a psychological fact": some people perceive "comprehension" as a physical action. "a generalization": people tend to gesture less with abstract concepts. "apparently disconfirming evidence": cases where the correlation seems to fail. "reconcile": show those cases fit after all, because the speaker treats the concept as physical.

The move to repeat: when an author defends a rule against exceptions by explaining why the exceptions are not what they seem, the Method answer will talk about reconciling or explaining away the counterevidence.

The author is not choosing among explanations for why people gesture. No rival explanation is named, and none is shown to be implausible. The argument defends the researchers' claim against apparent exceptions, which is a different job from eliminating alternatives.

E reverses the direction. The author argues the claim should not be rejected, not that it needs more support. E also calls the generalization "widely accepted," while the stimulus attributes it only to "Some researchers." The reason given is a reason the claim survives, not a reason to demand more evidence.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: The fact that the correlation between gesturing and talking about physical, rather than abstract, concepts is not a perfect correlation does not provide any grounds for rejecting that the correlation exists.

old_steps.label: Evidence (because)
old_steps.body: There are some words, such as 'comprehension', that are in a gray area. Some people feel them more like abstract concepts; others feel them more like physical concepts.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: So it sounds like some people, who interpret 'comprehension' more like a physical act of grasping something would be more likely to gesture when talking about it, whereas other people who interpret 'comprehension' more like an abstract concept would be less likely to gesture when talking about it. If a contrarian was saying, "Hey, researchers --- how come this person is gesturing while they're talking about the abstract concept of comprehension?", the researchers might say, "This person doesn't perceive comprehension as an abstract concept. They perceive it more as a physical act of grasping something, so their behavior does still accord with our correlation."

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: If we were trying to characterize this type of evidence by choosing from Method's Big 8 types of answers (analogy, counter/example of a general claim, implications of logic, ruling out alternatives, suggesting alternate explanation, raising overlooked consideration, calling out a dubious assumption, making a distinction or definition), we could use a couple of these: The author cites an example of a data point that could lead someone to challenge the researchers' correlation and then offers an alternate explanation for it, that would make ti more compatible with the researchers correlation (they're gesturing about 'comprehension' not because the researchers were wrong but because they think of 'comprehension' as a physical concept).

old_notes.body: The argument does not attempt to show that the correlation is universal. In fact, it explicitly acknowledges that the correlation is "far from universal." The argument's goal is to defend the generalization against the objection that non-universality disproves it — not to prove universality. The ambiguity of a word (like "comprehension") is cited to explain why apparent exceptions are not genuine counterexamples, not to establish that no exceptions exist. This answer mischaracterizes both the conclusion (the argument concedes non-universality) and the method (the argument reconciles, not universalizes).

The argument does not appeal to a universal psychological generalization to support a claim about gesturing. The psychological fact cited — that some people perceive "comprehension" as expressing physical action — is not universal. It is a specific observation about individual variation in concept categorization. The argument uses this particular psychological observation to explain apparent exceptions to the researchers' claim, not as a sweeping generalization about all human psychology. Furthermore, the argument is defending the researchers' claim, not establishing a new one. This answer mischaracterizes both the type of psychological evidence (particular, not universal) and the argumentative goal (defense, not support of a new claim).

The argument cites a psychological fact — that some people perceive words like "comprehension" as expressing physical actions rather than abstract states — to reconcile the researchers' generalization (people gesture less when discussing abstract concepts) with apparently disconfirming instances (cases where the correlation does not hold). The psychological fact explains why these cases are not genuine counterexamples: if someone perceives "comprehension" as physical, then gesturing while discussing it is actually consistent with the rule, not a violation of it. The method is reconciliation through reinterpretation: the exceptions look like exceptions only because we are miscategorizing what the speaker considers abstract. This answer precisely describes that strategy.

The argument does not attempt to demonstrate that other explanations are impossible. It provides a single explanation for the apparent exceptions and uses that to defend the generalization. There is no systematic elimination of alternative accounts. The argument does not even address alternative explanations for the gesture-abstraction correlation — it addresses alternative interpretations of the apparent counterexamples. "Advocating an explanation by demonstrating other possibilities are unlikely" describes process-of-elimination reasoning, which is not what happens here. The argument is constructive (here is why the exceptions are not real exceptions), not eliminative (here is why no other explanation works).

The argument's entire purpose is to DEFEND the generalization against the claim that it needs more support or should be rejected. This answer says the argument offers reasons for believing the generalization requires still more evidence. That is the exact opposite of what the argument does. The argument says: the apparent exceptions do not disprove the claim (because of individual variation in concept perception), so the non-universality objection fails. It is strengthening the generalization's position, not arguing that it needs additional evidence. This answer describes the objection the argument is responding to, not the argument's own method.
